questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has had a blocked nose and facial pain for a week. For 2 days her right eye has been swollen and painful, and today her vision in that eye is blurred. Her right eye is pushed forward, the conjunctiva is swollen, and she cannot fully open the lid. Her temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 108 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, proptosis, chemosis, reduced vision and reduced eye opening after sinusitis are red flags for orbital cellulitis.

clues: blocked nose and facial pain for a week
vision in that eye is blurred
steps.x: Sinusitis + **proptosis** + **chemosis** + **reduced vision** + fever = postseptal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Orbital cellulitis.

elim: Swelling at the medial canthus over the lacrimal sac, without proptosis.
Itchy, bilateral, afebrile, with no proptosis.
Vision and the globe position are normal in preseptal infection.
Proptosis without fever or acute sinusitis.

steps.x: **C. Orbital cellulitis.** Vision, movement or proptosis affected = orbital.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy has chickenpox. One spot on his left upper eyelid became red and crusted 3 days ago, and the whole lid is now swollen, red and tender. He is eating and playing. His temperature is 37.9°C. He follows a toy in all directions, the eye is not pushed forward and pupils react normally.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A red, swollen, tender eyelid after a skin infection with normal eye movements, pupils and no proptosis is periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis.

clues: follows a toy in all directions
steps.x: Skin infection on the lid, but the **eye itself is normal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Periorbital cellulitis.

elim: A painless lump in the lid, not diffuse red swelling.
Dermatomal vesicles in adults; he has a secondarily infected chickenpox spot.
Eye movements, pupils and globe position are normal.
A small tender lump at the lash line, not the whole lid.

steps.x: **D. Periorbital cellulitis.** Preseptal: eyelid only, eye normal.

questions.stem: An 8 year old girl had a cold last week. For 2 days her left eyelids have been swollen and red. Today she has a temperature of 38.9°C, a pulse rate of 128 bpm, and complains of seeing two of everything. Her parents think the left eye looks different from the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Bilateral eyelid oedema with normal eyes
Left fixed dilated pupil with ptosis
Left proptosis with restricted eye movements
Left ptosis with a small pupil
questions.e: Orbital cellulitis causes erythema and swelling, fever, pain, proptosis and diplopia from complex ophthalmoplegia.

steps.x: Diplopia + febrile child after URTI = **orbital**: expect proptosis and ophthalmoplegia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Proptosis with restricted movements.

elim: Suggests a systemic cause, not unilateral infection.
A third nerve palsy, not the usual orbital picture.
Horner's syndrome.
Diplopia means the movements are restricted.

steps.x: **C. Left proptosis with restricted eye movements.** Orbital: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, diplopia.

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy is on IV antibiotics for right orbital cellulitis. Over 12 hours his right acuity falls from 6/9 to 6/60 and he can no longer name the colours on a chart with that eye. There is a new right RAPD. The proptosis has increased.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his visual loss?
questions.e: Rising orbital pressure from infection or an abscess compresses the optic nerve, causing reduced acuity, colour loss and a RAPD.

steps.x: Falling acuity + **RAPD** + **rising proptosis** = the optic nerve is being squeezed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Compressive optic neuropathy.

elim: Not the mechanism in orbital infection.
Not typical; a RAPD with rising proptosis points to nerve compression.
Would not cause a RAPD.
Would affect both eyes, with no RAPD.

steps.x: **C. Compressive optic neuropathy.** Orbital cellulitis threatens vision via compressive optic neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 13 year old girl with left orbital cellulitis after frontal and ethmoid sinusitis has been on IV antibiotics for 2 days. She now has a severe headache, photophobia and vomiting. Her neck is stiff and she is drowsy. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 132 bpm and BP 102/60 mmHg. Both eyes move normally apart from the left.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Intracranial spread from orbital cellulitis can cause meningitis: headache, photophobia, neck stiffness and drowsiness.

clues: Both eyes move normally apart from the left
steps.x: **Meningism** with the other eye normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Meningitis.

elim: Would affect the other eye with bilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia.
Not with fever, neck stiffness and drowsiness.
A local orbital complication; it does not cause neck stiffness.
Not with fever and meningism.

steps.x: **B. Meningitis.** Complications: vision loss, abscess, CST, meningitis, intracranial spread.

questions.stem: An 11 year old boy is being treated for right orbital cellulitis. The team is watching for signs that the infection has spread backwards to the cavernous sinus. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 120 bpm. Five possible new findings are discussed.
questions.q: Which new finding would most suggest cavernous sinus thrombosis?
o: Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia of the left eye
questions.e: The cavernous sinuses communicate, so involvement of the other eye (bilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia) with headache suggests cavernous sinus thrombosis.

clues: spread backwards to the cavernous sinus
steps.x: The cavernous sinuses connect across the midline, so look for the **other eye**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Signs in the left eye.

elim: Local spread, not cavernous sinus.
Already part of orbital cellulitis.
Suggests sinusitis, the source.
Non-specific.

steps.x: **C. Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia of the left eye.** CST: the other eye becomes involved.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man had a blow-out fracture of the right orbital floor in a football collision 5 days ago. He now has worsening swelling and pain around the right eye, double vision and a temperature of 38.5°C. He has no sinus symptoms and no skin wound. His acuity is 6/9 right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor for his infection?
questions.e: Fracture of any of the orbital bones, here the floor (maxilla), predisposes to orbital cellulitis.

clues: blow-out fracture of the right orbital floor
no sinus symptoms and no skin wound
steps.x: No sinusitis, no wound, but a **fracture** into the orbit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The orbital fracture.

elim: Causes keratitis, not orbital infection.
No history given.
None reported.
He has no sinus or URTI symptoms.

steps.x: **D. Orbital bone fracture.** Orbital fracture predisposes to orbital cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has had left eyelid swelling for 2 days after a cold. His mother brings him back because he is now lethargic, has a headache and will not open the left eye. When the lid is lifted the conjunctiva is swollen. His temperature is 39.0°C and pulse rate 136 bpm. He will not cooperate with eye movement testing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Red flags for orbital cellulitis include systemic illness, headache, chemosis and reduced eye opening; if eye movements cannot be tested, treat as orbital.

clues: will not open the left eye
steps.x: **Systemic illness**, **headache**, **chemosis**, **reduced eye opening**: red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Orbital cellulitis.

elim: Afebrile, itchy, and the child is well.
A painless lid lump without fever or chemosis.
Sticky eye without systemic illness or reduced eye opening.
Systemic illness, chemosis, headache and reduced eye opening are orbital red flags.

steps.x: **D. Orbital cellulitis.** Red flags mean orbital, even if the eye cannot be fully examined.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has right proptosis, painful eye movements and fever after ethmoid sinusitis. Her parents ask the registrar why she needs to stay in hospital when her cousin with a swollen eyelid was sent home with tablets. Her temperature is 38.8°C.
questions.q: Which best describes the site of her infection?
o: In front of the orbital septum
questions.e: Orbital cellulitis is infection posterior to the orbital septum, threatening the globe, muscles and orbital apex, and is an ophthalmological emergency.

steps.x: Proptosis and painful movements = infection has passed the **septum**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Behind the septum (postseptal).

elim: Preseptal; her eye is involved.
Preseptal cellulitis.
Keratitis, with a red eye and normal globe position.
Dacryocystitis, medial canthal swelling.

steps.x: **A. Behind the orbital septum.** Orbital = postseptal = emergency.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman was stung by a wasp on her right upper eyelid 2 days ago. The lid is now red, warm and swollen, but she can open the eye. Her temperature is 37.6°C. She has no headache. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes.
questions.q: Which other finding is most likely on examination of the right eye?
questions.e: In periorbital cellulitis the septum protects the orbit, so vision, pupils and eye movements stay normal with no proptosis.

steps.x: Insect bite + lid swelling + **normal acuity** = preseptal. The rest of the eye is spared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Normal eye movements.

elim: Suggests optic nerve compression.
A red flag for orbital involvement.
Suggests ophthalmoplegia.
Proptosis is absent in preseptal cellulitis.

steps.x: **E. Full, painless eye movements.** Preseptal: vision, pupils, movements normal, no proptosis.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has left proptosis, chemosis, painful restricted eye movements and fever after a week of sinusitis. His acuity is 6/12 left. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 112 bpm. IV antibiotics have been started and the team want imaging to look for an abscess and intracranial spread.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain
questions.e: The best imaging is contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain, showing abscesses, the sinus source and intracranial spread.

clues: look for an abscess and intracranial spread
steps.x: Need **orbit**, **sinus** and **brain** in one scan, with contrast.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Contrast CT orbits, sinuses and brain.

elim: Misses orbital abscess and sinus detail.
Operator-dependent and cannot show intracranial spread.
Shows little and nothing of the orbit.
Not useful.

steps.x: **A. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain.** Best imaging: contrast CT orbits, sinuses, brain.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl arrives in the emergency department with a swollen, red right eye, fever and pain on eye movement after a cold. She has mild right proptosis. Her temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 130 bpm. The emergency doctor suspects orbital cellulitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial step?
o: Urgent ophthalmology and ENT review with blood tests
questions.e: Suspected orbital cellulitis needs clinical recognition plus urgent ophthalmology and ENT review and blood tests.

clues: pain on eye movement after a cold
steps.x: Suspected **orbital** = emergency: specialist review now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent ophthalmology and ENT review with bloods.

elim: Orbital cellulitis needs admission.
Far too slow for an emergency.
Delays emergency care.
Do not treat orbital infection.

steps.x: **E. Urgent ophthalmology and ENT review with blood tests.** Orbital cellulitis: urgent ophthalmology + ENT.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl has a red, swollen left lower eyelid after scratching an insect bite. She is afebrile and well. Visual acuity is 6/6, pupils react normally, eye movements are full and painless and there is no proptosis. Her father asks whether she needs a scan.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to investigation?
questions.e: Periorbital cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis after careful assessment excludes orbital signs; CT is reserved for suspected orbital cellulitis.

clues: eye movements are full and painless
steps.x: Every orbital sign is **absent**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical diagnosis, no imaging.

elim: Needed when orbital cellulitis is suspected, not here.
No meningism.
No neurological features.
Unhelpful.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis without imaging.** CT only when orbital involvement is suspected.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy is admitted with left orbital cellulitis after sinusitis. He has proptosis and painful eye movements. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. IV access is obtained and antibiotics are about to be given.
questions.q: Which blood tests are most appropriate before the antibiotics?
questions.e: Blood tests in orbital cellulitis assess infection (FBC, CRP) and try to identify the organism (blood cultures) before IV antibiotics.

clues: antibiotics are about to be given
steps.x: Infection markers + **cultures before antibiotics**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FBC, CRP, blood cultures.

elim: Not useful acutely.
For connective tissue disease.
Does not assess infection.
For haemolysis, not infection.

steps.x: **E. FBC, CRP and blood cultures.** Bloods before IV antibiotics: FBC, CRP, cultures.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a red, swollen, tender right upper eyelid after a spot on the lid became infected 2 days ago. She feels well. Her temperature is 37.5°C. Acuity is 6/6, eye movements are full and painless and there is no proptosis. She has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav with safety-netting and review
questions.e: Mild periorbital cellulitis in a well patient is treated with oral co-amoxiclav, close follow-up and safety-netting for orbital progression.

clues: eye movements are full and painless
steps.x: **Mild**, **well**, eye normal: oral treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral co-amoxiclav with safety-netting.

elim: For orbital cellulitis or a significant infection.
No abscess, and she is well.
Do not treat cellulitis of the lid.
Steroids do not treat infection.

steps.x: **D. Oral co-amoxiclav with safety-netting and review.** Mild preseptal: oral co-amoxiclav.

questions.stem: An 11 month old boy has a red, swollen left eyelid after a cold. He is irritable and feeding less. His temperature is 38.8°C and pulse rate 165 bpm. His eye appears to move normally when he follows a light, and there is no proptosis, but a full examination is difficult.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav and review in 1 week
questions.e: IV antibiotics are needed for periorbital cellulitis when there is paediatric concern, such as a febrile, irritable infant who is hard to examine.

steps.x: **Infant**, febrile, unwell, hard to examine = paediatric concern.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Admit for IV antibiotics.

elim: Too risky in a febrile infant with an incomplete exam.
Unsafe.
Inadequate for cellulitis.
No abscess has been shown.

steps.x: **A. Admit for intravenous antibiotics.** Paediatric concern = IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl with periorbital cellulitis after an insect bite is well enough to go home on oral co-amoxiclav. Her eye movements and vision are normal and there is no proptosis. Her temperature is 37.4°C. The doctor explains when to come back.
questions.q: Which is the most important safety-net advice?
o: Return if she develops a cough
Return if she has eye pain, double vision, reduced vision or a bulging eye
Return if the lid is still pink after a day
Return only if she cannot eat for a week
Return only if the rash spreads to her cheek
questions.e: Safety-net all patients for orbital progression: eye pain, diplopia, reduced vision or proptosis indicate orbital cellulitis.

steps.x: What signs mean the infection has gone **behind the septum**?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pain, diplopia, reduced vision, proptosis.

elim: Not relevant to orbital spread.
Expected; not a warning sign.
Too late.
Misses orbital warning signs.

steps.x: **B. Return if she has eye pain, double vision, reduced vision or a bulging eye.** Safety-net for orbital signs.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has orbital cellulitis of the left eye with proptosis and painful restricted eye movements. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin last year and a rash with a cephalosporin. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is admitted.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Orbital cellulitis needs admission and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics such as cefotaxime or clindamycin; with penicillin and cephalosporin allergy, clindamycin is used.

steps.x: IV broad-spectrum options: **cefotaxime or clindamycin**. One is excluded by allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV clindamycin.

elim: She reacted to a cephalosporin.
Contains penicillin; she had anaphylaxis.
Oral therapy is inadequate for orbital cellulitis.
Does not treat orbital infection.

steps.x: **B. Intravenous clindamycin.** Orbital: admit, IV cefotaxime or clindamycin.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy is admitted with right orbital cellulitis after ethmoid sinusitis. CT shows a subperiosteal abscess along the medial orbital wall. He has started IV cefotaxime. His acuity is 6/9 right. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 122 bpm.
questions.q: Which teams should urgently review him?
questions.e: Orbital cellulitis needs urgent ophthalmology (vision) and ENT (sinus source, surgical drainage if needed) review.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl is admitted with left orbital cellulitis. Her parents ask why she cannot just take antibiotic medicine by mouth at home like her brother did for an ear infection. Her temperature is 38.5°C and pulse rate 128 bpm.

o: Oral antibiotics do not reach the skin

questions.e: IV antibiotics are needed in orbital cellulitis because of the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread.

steps.x: Orbital infection can spread **backwards** to the brain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Risk of CST and intracranial spread.

It is bacterial.
Not the reason.
They do; this is about the danger of spread.

steps.x: **E. Risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread.** IV because of CST and intracranial risk.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy is brought to the GP with a red, swollen right upper eyelid for a day after a cold. His temperature is 37.8°C. He is playing in the waiting room. The GP has not yet examined the eye.
questions.q: Which is the most important first step in assessment?

questions.e: The first step in periorbital cellulitis is careful assessment to rule out orbital cellulitis: vision, pupils, eye movements and proptosis.

steps.x: First decide: **preseptal or orbital**?

steps.x: Examine vision, pupils, movements and proptosis.

Only if orbital cellulitis is suspected.
Does not change initial management.
Not before deciding preseptal or orbital.

steps.x: **A. Check vision, pupils, eye movements and for proptosis.** Rule out orbital cellulitis first.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has periorbital cellulitis that began at an infected cut on his left eyebrow from a fall 3 days ago. The lid is red and swollen with a little pus at the wound. His temperature is 37.9°C. Eye movements and vision are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Periocular infection after a skin wound is most often Staphylococcus aureus (or Streptococcus pyogenes); S. pneumoniae is typical after ethmoid sinusitis in children.

clues: infected cut on his left eyebrow
a little pus at the wound
steps.x: Skin wound + **pus** = **S. aureus**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Staphylococcus aureus.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** Organisms: S. aureus, S. pyogenes, S. pneumoniae.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy develops left orbital cellulitis 5 days after starting with a cold and a blocked nose. He has no skin wound or bite. His temperature is 38.8°C. CT shows an opacified left ethmoid sinus next to a medial orbital collection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of infection into the orbit?
o: Contiguous spread from the ethmoid sinus
Direct inoculation through the eyelid skin

steps.x: Sinus next to the collection, no skin route: **contiguous** spread.

steps.x: Contiguous spread from the ethmoid sinus.

Not adjacent to the orbit.

steps.x: **B. Contiguous spread from the ethmoid sinus.** Usual route: contiguous from the paranasal sinuses.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has a very swollen, red right upper eyelid after an insect bite. When the lid is gently lifted, her eye is white, acuity is 6/6, pupils react normally and eye movements are full and painless. A student asks why the infection has not reached the eye.

questions.e: The orbital septum separates the preseptal and postseptal compartments; while intact it keeps infection away from the globe, muscles and orbital apex.

eye movements are full and painless
steps.x: Severe lid swelling but a **normal eye**: a barrier is holding.

steps.x: The orbital septum.

steps.x: **D. Orbital septum.** Septum integrity decides preseptal vs orbital.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy has right orbital cellulitis. He sees double when looking to the right and up, and moving the eye in any direction is painful. His acuity is 6/9 right with no RAPD. His temperature is 38.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his double vision?

questions.e: Orbital infection and oedema restrict the extraocular muscles, causing ophthalmoplegia and diplopia; compression of the optic nerve causes reduced acuity and a RAPD.

clues: sees double when looking to the right and up
moving the eye in any direction is painful
steps.x: Diplopia in several directions = **muscles** restricted by inflamed orbital tissue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Extraocular muscle restriction.
